title: WWII Timeline — From Blitzkrieg to Surrender
subtitle: Dual-theater World War II chronology with home front developments (Sep 1939 – Sep 1945)

events.headline: Germany Invades Poland
events.short: Blitzkrieg begins; Britain and France declare war on Germany.
events.long: On September 1, 1939, German forces launched a coordinated air, armor, and infantry assault on Poland, demonstrating the devastating speed of Blitzkrieg tactics. Britain and France honored their guarantees to Poland and declared war on September 3, marking the formal start of World War II in Europe. Soviet forces invaded eastern Poland on September 17 under the secret terms of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, and Poland was partitioned within weeks.
events.connection: Sets the pattern for Axis aggression that culminates in the Fall of France and Operation Barbarossa.

events.headline: Fall of France
events.short: Germany sweeps through the Low Countries and France in six weeks.
events.long: German armored columns pushed through the Ardennes, bypassing the Maginot Line and trapping Allied forces against the English Channel. The British Expeditionary Force was evacuated at Dunkirk while Paris fell on June 14. France signed an armistice on June 22, leaving Britain to face Germany alone. The collapse stunned the world and made an isolationist United States re-examine its position.
events.connection: The defeat of France isolated Britain and set the stage for the Battle of Britain and the Blitz.

events.headline: The Blitz
events.short: Sustained German bombing of British cities fails to break morale.
events.long: Unable to gain air superiority for an invasion, Hitler shifted the Luftwaffe to nighttime terror bombing of London, Coventry, and other British cities. Over eight months, more than 40,000 British civilians were killed, but production continued and civilian morale held. The RAF's defense and the resilience of British cities denied Germany a decisive victory in the West and pushed Hitler toward his fateful turn east.
events.connection: Failure of the Blitz contributed to Hitler's decision to invade the Soviet Union in Operation Barbarossa.

events.headline: Operation Barbarossa
events.short: Germany launches the largest military invasion in history against the USSR.
events.long: Over three million Axis troops poured across a 1,800-mile front from the Baltic to the Black Sea, breaking the Nazi–Soviet Pact and opening a second European front. Early gains were enormous, but the Red Army absorbed the blow, factories were relocated east of the Urals, and the Wehrmacht stalled outside Moscow as winter set in. Barbarossa committed Germany to a two-front war it could not sustain.
events.connection: Turning point: opened the Eastern Front that would consume most of Germany's army and ultimately bleed it dry, while bringing the USSR into the Allied coalition.

events.headline: Pearl Harbor
events.short: Japanese surprise attack brings the United States into the war.
events.long: On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese carrier aircraft struck the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging eight battleships and killing more than 2,400 Americans. President Roosevelt called it 'a date which will live in infamy,' and Congress declared war on Japan the next day. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11, transforming separate regional conflicts into a global war.
events.connection: Turning point: ended American isolationism and aligned the U.S. with Britain and the USSR, dramatically shifting the balance of industrial power against the Axis.

events.headline: War Production Board
events.short: Federal agency converts U.S. industry to wartime production.
events.long: Established by executive order in January 1942, the War Production Board directed the conversion of civilian factories to military output, allocated scarce raw materials, and set production priorities. Automobile plants began turning out tanks and bombers; consumer goods like new cars and refrigerators disappeared from stores. By 1944 the United States was producing more war material than all the Axis powers combined.
events.connection: Industrial mobilization that armed the Allies on every front, from Sherman tanks in Europe to Essex-class carriers in the Pacific.

events.headline: Executive Order 9066 — Japanese Internment
events.short: Roosevelt authorizes the forced relocation of Japanese Americans.
events.long: Signed February 19, 1942, Executive Order 9066 authorized military commanders to designate exclusion zones, leading to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry — most of them U.S. citizens — from the West Coast to inland concentration camps. Families lost homes, businesses, and farms. The Supreme Court upheld the program in Korematsu v. United States, a decision later widely condemned as a grave civil-liberties failure.
events.connection: Stands as a cautionary counterpoint to Allied rhetoric about freedom and democracy, and shaped postwar civil-rights debates.

events.headline: Battle of Midway
events.short: U.S. carrier strike sinks four Japanese carriers and reverses Pacific momentum.
events.long: Acting on broken Japanese naval codes, the U.S. Pacific Fleet ambushed a Japanese force aimed at Midway Atoll. Dive bombers from USS Enterprise, Hornet, and Yorktown destroyed the carriers Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu in a single afternoon, gutting Japan's elite naval air arm. The Imperial Japanese Navy never recovered its offensive initiative.
events.connection: Turning point: shifted the strategic initiative in the Pacific from Japan to the United States and made the island-hopping campaign possible.

events.headline: Guadalcanal Campaign
events.short: First major U.S. land offensive in the Pacific secures the Solomon Islands.
events.long: U.S. Marines landed on Guadalcanal in August 1942 to deny Japan an airfield within bomber range of Australia. Six months of brutal jungle, naval, and air combat followed before Japanese forces evacuated in February 1943. The campaign exhausted Japanese aircraft, pilots, and ships at a rate they could not replace.
events.connection: First step in the island-hopping strategy that would eventually carry U.S. forces to Saipan, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa.

events.headline: Rosie the Riveter — "We Can Do It!"
events.short: Iconic poster captures the wartime mobilization of American women.
events.long: J. Howard Miller's 'We Can Do It!' poster, produced for Westinghouse in February 1943, became a lasting symbol of the millions of American women who entered defense factories, shipyards, and offices to replace men sent to war. Female employment in manufacturing rose sharply, and women operated lathes, welded ship hulls, and built aircraft. Many were laid off after V-J Day, but the experience reshaped expectations about women's roles.
events.connection: Helped enable the production miracle directed by the War Production Board and changed long-term patterns of women's work and citizenship.

events.headline: War Refugee Board
events.short: Belated U.S. effort to rescue Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution.
events.long: Created by executive order in January 1944 after years of restrictive immigration policy, the War Refugee Board worked with neutral countries and private agencies to rescue refugees from Nazi-occupied Europe. Its agents, including Raoul Wallenberg in Budapest, helped save an estimated 200,000 lives. The board's late creation underscores how slowly the U.S. responded to the Holocaust.
events.connection: Frames the moral context for Allied military campaigns in 1944–45 and informs postwar debates about responsibility and refugees.

events.headline: D-Day — Normandy Invasion
events.short: Largest amphibious assault in history opens the Western Front.
events.long: On June 6, 1944, more than 156,000 Allied troops landed on five Normandy beaches under General Dwight D. Eisenhower's overall command. Despite heavy casualties at Omaha Beach, the lodgement held; by late August, Allied forces had broken out, liberated Paris, and driven German forces back toward the Rhine. D-Day finally opened the second front Stalin had long demanded.
events.connection: Turning point: forced Germany to fight a full-scale two-front war and put Allied armies on a path to Berlin.

events.headline: Battle of Saipan
events.short: Marianas victory puts Tokyo in range of American B-29 bombers.
events.long: U.S. Marines and Army troops took Saipan after three weeks of intense combat in which more than 3,000 Americans and most of the 30,000-strong Japanese garrison were killed. Capture of the island and nearby Tinian gave the United States airbases within B-29 range of the Japanese home islands. The fall of Saipan brought down the Tojo government in Tokyo.
events.connection: Set the stage for the strategic bombing of Japan and for the Iwo Jima and Okinawa campaigns.

events.headline: Battle of the Bulge
events.short: Last major German offensive on the Western Front fails in the Ardennes.
events.long: In a desperate winter counterattack, German armored forces drove a 'bulge' into thinly held American lines in the Ardennes, hoping to split the Allied armies and seize the port of Antwerp. The 101st Airborne held Bastogne under siege, Patton's Third Army wheeled north, and the offensive was stopped within weeks. Germany lost irreplaceable tanks, aircraft, and men.
events.connection: Exhausted Germany's remaining reserves and accelerated the Allied advance to the Rhine and into Germany itself.

events.headline: Battle of Iwo Jima
events.short: Marines take a fiercely defended island for emergency B-29 landings.
events.long: U.S. Marines fought their way across eight square miles of volcanic ash against an entrenched Japanese garrison that had largely abandoned beach defense for tunnels and pillboxes. The flag-raising atop Mount Suribachi on February 23 became an enduring image of American sacrifice. Nearly 7,000 Marines were killed; almost all 21,000 Japanese defenders died.
events.connection: Demonstrated the rising cost of assaulting the Japanese home islands and intensified debate about how to end the war.

events.headline: Battle of Okinawa
events.short: Bloodiest Pacific battle previews the cost of invading Japan.
events.long: American forces seized Okinawa, only 350 miles from Kyushu, in 82 days of combat that killed more than 12,000 Americans, around 100,000 Japanese soldiers, and at least 100,000 Okinawan civilians. Kamikaze attacks sank 36 U.S. ships. Planners projected even higher casualties for an invasion of the home islands, sharpening the appeal of alternatives.
events.connection: Casualty projections from Okinawa weighed heavily on the decision to drop the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

events.headline: Germany Surrenders (V-E Day)
events.short: Unconditional surrender ends the war in Europe.
events.long: After Soviet forces seized Berlin and Adolf Hitler killed himself on April 30, German military leaders signed an unconditional surrender at Reims on May 7 and again in Berlin on May 8. Crowds celebrated V-E Day across Allied capitals while occupation zones were established under agreements reached at Yalta. Roughly 40 million Europeans had died, and the continent lay in ruins.
events.connection: Closed the European war and freed Allied resources for the final campaign against Japan; foreshadowed the Cold War division of Europe.

events.headline: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.short: Atomic bombings devastate two Japanese cities and hasten surrender.
events.long: On August 6, 1945, the B-29 Enola Gay dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, killing an estimated 70,000 people instantly; tens of thousands more died from burns and radiation. Three days later a second bomb destroyed Nagasaki. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria on August 8. Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on August 15.
events.connection: Turning point: opened the nuclear age, ended World War II without an invasion of the home islands, and set the terms for Cold War deterrence.

events.headline: Japan Surrenders (V-J Day)
events.short: Formal surrender aboard USS Missouri ends World War II.
events.long: Japanese officials signed the Instrument of Surrender on the deck of USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945, formally ending six years of global war. General Douglas MacArthur presided as Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers and began an occupation that would last until 1952. More than 60 million people had died worldwide; the United States emerged as the dominant industrial and military power.
events.connection: Closes the WWII timeline and opens the postwar era of decolonization, the United Nations, and the Cold War.
